Why I’m Using
Dr.
From Here on out
By
Leslie Camhi
December 17, 2020
An photo of the author taken during a year she spent researching her dissertation in Paris, circa 1990.
Photo: courtesy of Leslie Camhi

Recently, on Instagram, I changed my identity—or rather, I reclaimed a part of my personal history that I’d kept, not exactly secret, but in a state of suspended animation for years. During the past few weeks, to my small but still (to me, at least) significant legion of followers, I have been known as Dr. Leslie Camhi.
A few followers reached out to me, asking whether I’d suddenly acquired new academic credentials. No, I told them, I hadn’t gone back to school. In fact, the doctoral dissertation—242 pages, not including illustrations—with which I’d earned my Ph.D. in comparative literature from Yale University had been gathering dust on my bookshelf for decades. Having received my degree at the height of the economic recession in the early 1990s, I spent a few fruitless years on the academic job market, juggling postdocs and adjunct teaching while beginning a career of writing for newspapers and magazines.
My education remained a point of pride—and it informed almost everything I wrote. But I rarely spoke of it, and I never used my title. In truth, there was much about my years of studying literary theory—the intensely analytical approach to language, the widely touted death of the author—that was crippling, creatively. There were lessons from those years that I had to unlearn in order to find my voice. And then the credential seemed superfluous to the urgent task which lay before me each day, of slinging words together while on deadline.
Until last month, that is, when in honor of our incoming first lady—Dr. Jill Biden—I adopted the honorific that, all these many years, had been mine to claim. Dr. Biden earned her doctorate in education, or Ed.D., in 2007 from the University of Delaware. The thrill I’d felt back in August, watching her address the Democratic National Convention from the empty classroom of a high school where she’d once taught English, had helped sustain me through a New York City autumn which included a return to remote school and online-only college tours for my high school senior; doomsday scrolling as our local infection rates ticked upward; and the slow torture of an “Election Day” that dragged on for almost a week.
I’d winced two years earlier at the agrammatical slogan with which first lady Melania Trump had introduced her (still largely unrealized) initiative to improve U.S. children’s lives. (“Be Better,” or “Be
the
Best,” but
not
“Be Best!”) In Dr. Biden, I saw a woman who knew her way around a blackboard, who had probably spent countless unglamorous hours offering feedback on homework, and who had taught for years at community college, even while serving as second lady during the Obama presidency.
My hope was that, with a doctor of education in the White House, this country’s long-ailing educational system—which has been struggling on life support through much of the pandemic—would finally move to the forefront of national concern.
In Dr. Biden, I saw a woman who knew her way around a blackboard, who had probably spent countless unglamorous hours offering feedback on homework.
And then, with the pandemic, I found myself, like many people, living a little more in my head. It’s true, I’m not an emergency worker or first responder—the only ills my kind of Dr. can tend to are logical fallacies, run-on sentences, and the like. But I felt the time had come for me to own my elaborate education, without shame or regrets, and acknowledge its central place in my life.
Well, that old feminist saw, “the personal is political,” came back to haunt me last weekend, when Joseph Epstein (a former adjunct professor at Northwestern)
published a now notorious essay
in the opinion pages of the
Wall Street Journal
, decrying Dr. Biden’s use of her title as “fraudulent, even comic.” Epstein referred to Dr. Biden as “kiddo” and deemed her dissertation’s title “unpromising.” (That dissertation focused on ways to retain students enrolled in community colleges, where—lamentably—six out of 10 students drop out before completing their degrees.) He didn’t bother to read it. After casting multiple aspersions—on community college students, on recent recipients of honorary doctorates, on the field of educational research itself—he advised the spouse of our current president-elect to abandon
Dr.
in favor of the title that her husband and a majority of Americans had bestowed upon her—
madame first lady.
Of course, Epstein’s essay provoked a firestorm of criticism in both social and mainstream media. A lawyer pal who works for an environmental nonprofit, channeling Margaret Atwood, called the
Journal
“Gilead’s paper of record,” and bitterly suggested that, in place of “Mrs. Biden,” our soon-to-be first lady might consider “OfJoe” as an option. An English professor at a prominent Northeast university (who, like most of my academic friends, has a Ph.D. but never uses his title) began posting the names of famous “doctors” in literature, their honorifics changed to “Mister” (“Mister Faust,” “Mr. Johnson,” etc.), all of which left me pondering the author Theodor Geisel, who received an honorary doctorate in humane letters from Dartmouth (his undergraduate alma mater) in 1955. Shall we now refer to him as “
Mr
. Seuss?”
Mr. Epstein, unlike you, I did complete my doctorate. (And since in your essay, you make a point of writing that you were never elected to Phi Beta Kappa, I’ll admit that I’m a member of that club too.) Dearly departed, distinguished professors, Harold Bloom and Edward Said (the latter on a one-semester leave from Columbia), sat on my oral examination committee, questioning me on the poetry of Paul Celan and Emily Dickinson, and the essayists of the Frankfurt School.

My dissertation (whose title I am not foolish enough to cite here) on hysteria, the naturalist novel, 19th-century French medical photography and the origins of psychoanalysis in Paris—earned me a postdoctoral fellowship at the Pembroke Center for Teaching and Research on Women at Brown University. During that year of reprieve I completed and published the essay that remains, to date, my major contribution to academic literature, on fin de siècle, female kleptomania and the rise of the department store. (I’ve been told it’s widely cited.)
I can’t say for sure that sexism played a role in my failure, despite these credentials, to procure a tenure-track teaching position. Many other factors were undoubtedly involved. I was also the first person in my family to complete a four-year college degree, for example, and for me to join the academy’s thin-air club may have required “schooling” of a different sort.
But I am certain that the grace accorded to Joseph Epstein, to teach for 30 years at a major university without a Ph.D., would never have been given to me.
For now, at least, I’m keeping my title, presumptuous and unfashionable though it may appear. Other friends are experimenting with eyeliner or letting their hair go gray. We can all benefit from a little self-transformation in COVID times, no? As for me, I’ll own my education. And if anyone wants to learn about 19th-century department store kleptomania, I’m
@drlesliecamhi.
Please find me there.
